articles.title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Supply-Chain Attack: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 Steal Cloud Credentials
articles.context: A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1
articles.full_text:
A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were injected with credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud identity tokens, API keys, and sensitive credentials from developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud build hosts. Due to the package’s approximately 190,000 monthly downloads and the breadth of targeted credentials, immediate remediation is required for any environment that installed the compromised versions.

Agent-framework compromise at a glance

Affected package: agent-framework on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2

Last clean version: 1.26.0

Not affected: agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages

Exposure window: November 17, 2026, 20:35 to approximately 21:20 UTC

Payload: a Python .pth startup hook that harvests credentials on every interpreter launch

Exfiltration: zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL

Status: malicious versions quarantined by PyPI; no CVE assigned

What happened in the agent-framework supply-chain attack

Both malicious versions were published within a 33-minute window on November 17, 2026 (20:35 to 21:08 UTC) and removed by approximately 21:20 UTC.

The attack was entirely in packaging. Neither malicious release changed Agent Framework code or pulled in a rogue dependency. Instead, each version added a Python .pth startup hook file that executes on every Python interpreter launch, even if Agent Framework is never imported.

How the .pth startup hook runs and evades detection

The collector forks a detached background process, sets a flag to prevent re-execution in child processes, and silently harvests credentials. Version 1.26.2 restored the legitimate __init__.py byte-for-byte to evade diff-based detection while moving the payload to a new top-level module.

What credentials does the agent-framework malware steal?

The malware actively requested fresh credential tokens rather than only copying stored secrets. Targeted credentials include:

Environment variables matching sensitive substrings (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, and more) from the current process and up to 300 other processes via /proc/*/environ

Azure managed-identity tokens for 12 Azure resources (ARM, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, ML, AI Foundry, Container Registry, Azure DevOps) via IMDS and identity endpoints

Azure DevOps SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and OIDC tokens for federated identity

GitHub Actions OIDC tokens (version 1.26.2 only) when workflows have id-token: write permissions

Credential files including Azure CLI state, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, and .env files

All harvested data was exfiltrated via zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL.

Which agent-framework versions and environments are affected?

The following components are affected: agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI. The last clean version is 1.26.0. The dependency agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages were checked and are not affected.

Any environment that installed the compromised versions during the exposure window is at risk, including through loose version pins such as agent-framework>=1.26. This spans developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions), and cloud build hosts running Python.

At the time of writing, the malicious versions have been quarantined by PyPI and the Microsoft publisher account has been secured. No CVE has been assigned.

Why stolen cloud and CI/CD credentials raise the stakes

Successful exploitation allows attackers to obtain cloud identity tokens that grant access to Azure resources, steal CI/CD pipeline secrets that could enable lateral movement across repositories and infrastructure, and harvest stored credentials that could lead to full infrastructure compromise across multiple cloud providers.

The attack also demonstrates sophisticated evasion techniques, including restoring legitimate code to bypass diff-based reviews while hiding the payload in a separate module.

How to remediate the agent-framework compromise

Organizations should take the following remediation steps immediately:

Isolate affected hosts and CI runners.

Detect exposure by searching lockfiles, container images, CI caches, and environments for versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, and look for .pth files (agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth) and payload modules in site-packages.

Pin to agent-framework==1.26.0 with hash verification and rebuild from clean environments.

Rotate all credentials that may have been exposed, including Azure service principal credentials, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, GitHub tokens, npm/PyPI/Hugging Face tokens, Docker registry credentials, and any secrets in environment variables or .env files.

Audit Azure Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure DevOps audit logs, and GitHub Actions workflow runs for unauthorized access since November 17.

Hunt for IOCs by searching proxy and DNS logs for connections to webhook.site, User-Agent strings “af-runtime-diagnostics/1” and “runtime-diagnostics/1”, and bursts of IMDS token requests.

Block versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 at your package proxy and consider blocking webhook.site at the network level.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

Package versions: agent-framework 1.26.1, 1.26.2

Files in site-packages: agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth

Network: outbound connections to webhook.site

User-Agent strings: “af-runtime-diagnostics/1”, “runtime-diagnostics/1”

Behavior: bursts of IMDS token requests

How Orca helps detect compromised agent-framework packages

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable package versions, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize the risks that matter most. Orca’s SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scanning capabilities can detect compromised packages in cloud workloads. Customers running Orca’s agentless scanning should check whether their workloads contain the affected versions. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first.

Because this payload targets build hosts and pipelines as much as production, coverage has to start before deployment. Orca helps teams catch risky code before it reaches production. And because the real damage comes from what stolen tokens can reach, Orca also helps teams reduce identity-based cloud risk and detect and respond to cloud threats that follow a credential compromise. As agent frameworks become a recurring supply-chain target, securing AI systems means securing the packages they are built on.

articles.title: Two Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026
articles.full_text:
F5 has disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both in the HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module). Both are rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 (8.1 under CVSS 3.1) and can be triggered remotely without authentication on NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled. Successful exploitation can crash NGINX worker processes, corrupt memory and potentially lead to remote code execution on the server.

NGINX is one of the most widely deployed web servers and reverse proxies, often sitting in front of multiple websites and APIs. Because the flaws are in NGINX itself, applications behind an affected NGINX instance can be exposed even when their own code is secure. One of the flaws, CVE-2026-123007, dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, released in 2015. The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026.

NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

CVE-2026-123633 (use-after-free, CWE-416); CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow leading to heap buffer overflow, CWE-191 / CWE-787)

Severity

CVSS 4.0: 9.2 (Critical); CVSS 3.1: 8.1 (High) for both

Component

NGINX HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module)

Attack

Remote, unauthenticated, no user interaction

Required configuration

HTTP/2 enabled. CVE-2026-123633 additionally requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend and the worker process to be running low on worker_connections

Affected NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 and later; CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 and later (up to the fixed releases below)

Fixed NGINX Open Source

1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline)

Affected / fixed NGINX Plus

R33 and later; fixed in 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (see version table below)

Workaround

Disable HTTP/2 until patched

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 is available

What are CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007?

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety flaws in how NGINX processes HTTP/2 traffic.

CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2 connection use-after-free). NGINX keeps a list of idle connections that it may close when it runs out of free connection slots. An HTTP/2 connection could remain on this “reusable” list even after a new request stream started on it. When NGINX is proxying the request to a backend and is running low on worker_connections, it can close and free that connection while the request is still using it, resulting in a use-after-free in the worker process. The fix resets the connection’s reusable status when a new stream is created.

CVE-2026-123007 (HTTP/2 flow-control integer underflow). When an HTTP/2 stream is terminated, its unsent data is credited back to the connection’s flow-control window. A client could cause this window to exceed its allowed maximum, which breaks NGINX’s buffer size accounting and leads to an out-of-bounds memory write (heap buffer overflow), typically followed by a worker crash. Unlike CVE-2026-123633, this flaw does not require a backend: according to the researchers, it can also affect NGINX instances that only serve static content over HTTP/2. The fix accounts for queued frames when validating the client’s WINDOW_UPDATE.

According to F5, both flaws can lead to denial of service and memory corruption, and code execution is possible on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is disabled or can be bypassed. Researchers who reported the issues state that they were able to achieve code execution, including bypassing ASLR, on standard 64-bit systems. Both issues affect the data plane only; F5 reports no control-plane exposure.

Which NGINX versions are affected?

Any NGINX deployment with HTTP/2 enabled that runs an affected version should be considered vulnerable. Versions on branches that have reached End of Technical Support are not evaluated by F5; they should be upgraded to a supported fixed release.

Product

CVE

Affected versions

Fixed versions

NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123633

1.19.7 and later, including 1.30.0 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8

1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)

NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123007

1.9.5 and later, including 1.30.0 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8

1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)

NGINX Plus

CVE-2026-123633

R33 and later; 37.0.0 before 37.0.7.1; 37.1.0 before 37.2.0.1

37.0.7.1, 37.2.0.1

NGINX Plus

CVE-2026-123007

R33 and later; 37.0.0 before 37.0.8.1; 37.1.0 before 37.3.0.1

37.0.8.1, 37.3.0.1

To address both vulnerabilities, NGINX Open Source users should move to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, and NGINX Plus users to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. Products and container images that bundle NGINX may also be affected; check the relevant vendor’s advisory for their fixed builds.

Additional NGINX vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

The same F5 security release also fixes three other critical NGINX vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. They do not involve HTTP/2, so disabling HTTP/2 does not mitigate them. Upgrading to NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or to NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, fixes all five vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-123634: a use-after-free when NGINX is configured as a proxy, the proxied server name includes variables, and a Server Side Includes (SSI) or mirror subrequest is sent to a location that resolves the same server name. Affects NGINX Open Source 0.6.18 and later.

CVE-2026-121810: a use-after-free in configurations that use HTTP/3. Affects NGINX Open Source 1.25.0 and later.

CVE-2026-113425: a use-after-free when NGINX is configured as a mail proxy. Affects NGINX Open Source 0.5.33 and later.

Is there a patch for the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities?

Yes. F5 released fixes on November 18, 2026: NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline), and NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1 address CVE-2026-123633 only). Linux distributions and other vendors that package NGINX release updates on their own schedules, so organizations using distribution packages or bundled NGINX should track their vendor’s advisory.

How to mitigate the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities before patching

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances, which blocks both vulnerabilities:

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in the affected server blocks.

On all versions, remove the http2 parameter from listen directives.

Reload NGINX, confirm that old worker processes have exited, and test application compatibility. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Additional recommended steps:

Inventory all NGINX deployments, including reverse proxies, load balancers, ingress layers and container images, and identify which have HTTP/2 enabled.

Prioritize internet-facing instances, and those that proxy traffic to backends.

Monitor for unexpected NGINX worker crashes or processes launched by NGINX, which can be general signs of exploitation attempts.

Are the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, there are no reports of in-the-wild exploitation. However, public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 has been released, including a script that triggers the flaw and an exploit demonstrating unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable NGINX server in a lab environment. Together with the detailed technical write-ups published alongside the disclosure, this significantly shortens the time to working exploits. Given how widely NGINX is exposed to the internet, organizations should treat these vulnerabilities as urgent.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable NGINX versions, including NGINX installed from OS packages and NGINX bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s runtime sensor can also help detect post-exploitation activity on affected hosts.

articles.title: “Java4Shell”: Critical OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Flaw Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: A critical vulnerability dubbed “Java4Shell” (CVE-2026-114938) has been reported in OpenJDK
articles.full_text:
A critical vulnerability dubbed “Java4Shell” (CVE-2026-114938) has been reported in OpenJDK. According to early reports, it lets unauthenticated attackers achieve remote code execution by sending a crafted Base64 string to a Java application running on x86 servers with AVX-512 support. Early reports rate it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. Java runs a large share of enterprise and cloud backends, so organizations should start inventorying their Java runtimes now and prepare to patch as soon as vendor builds are confirmed.

Security firm Calif, which says it discovered and reported the flaw, disclosed it publicly on November 17 because the details had already leaked, and says it will publish full technical details later that day, after Oracle releases its patch. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group has published an advisory that names this CVE, and as of this writing CVE records are only reserved but unpublished . [VERIFY @23:00]

Java4Shell key facts

Fact

Detail

CVE

CVE-2026-114938 [VERIFY @23:00: no CVE.org/NVD record yet]

Severity

9.2 (CVSS 4.0, per early reports)

Type

Reported heap buffer overflow in OpenJDK’s intrinsic Base64 decoder, leading to unauthenticated RCE

Likely affected

OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later; JDK 18+ lines contain the same code (scope unconfirmed)

Unlikely affected

Java 8 and 11; ARM-based hosts

Hardware

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI for the reported path

Patch

Oracle Nov 17 builds released; CVE not yet confirmed among fixes

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation or public PoC

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

The issue is a memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder, the native code the JVM uses in place of the Java implementation of java.util.Base64 decoding on supported CPUs. A crafted 65-byte input reportedly causes an integer underflow in padding handling. The result is a 62-byte heap buffer overflow that can corrupt adjacent Java objects and lead to code execution. Base64 decoding of untrusted input is very common in Java applications (such as authentication headers, tokens and encoded API payloads), so the reachable attack surface can be large. Exploitation still requires attacker-controlled data to reach the decoder.

Which Java versions could be affected by Java4Shell?

Public reports so far say “OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later”. Orca Research reviewed the OpenJDK source history to see which Java versions contain the reported vulnerable code. Containing the code does not by itself confirm that a version is exploitable; confirmation is expected once full technical details and vendor advisories are published:

The 17.0.6 boundary matches the code. The AVX-512 Base64 decoding intrinsic (JDK-8268276) was backported to the JDK 17 update line in November 2022 and first shipped in OpenJDK 17.0.6 (January 2023). It is not present in 17.0.5.

Newer Java lines likely carry the same code. The same decoder was added to mainline OpenJDK in 2021 and first released in JDK 18. JDK 21, 25 and 27 therefore contain it. Early reports mention only Java 17, and it has not been confirmed whether these newer lines are affected; until Oracle or OpenJDK clarifies the scope, organizations may want to treat them as potentially exposed. [VERIFY @23:00]

Java 8 and 11 do not contain this decoder intrinsic in OpenJDK, so they are unlikely to be affected by Java4Shell. Oracle released updates for these lines on November 17 (8u513 and 11.0.33.1) as part of the same patch update.

Hardware matters. On Java 17, the Base64 intrinsic is enabled only on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512; on Java 21 and later it is also enabled on CPUs with AVX2. However, the AVX-512 decoding path that early reports point to runs only on CPUs with the AVX-512 VBMI extension (e.g., Intel Ice Lake and later, AMD Zen 4 and later). ARM-based hosts (e.g., AWS Graviton) use different decoder code and are not known to be affected.

All distributions are in scope. The code is in upstream OpenJDK, so Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat and distro OpenJDK packages built from affected versions should all be considered potentially affected, including JDKs bundled inside applications and container images.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-114938?

On November 17, Oracle released new builds for Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25 and 27 (8u513, 11.0.33.1, 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1) as part of its November Critical Security Patch Update. According to Oracle’s pre-release announcement, the update contains 11 Java SE fixes, all remotely exploitable without authentication (highest CVSS 3.1 score 8.1). The 9.2 figure in early reports is a CVSS 4.0 score, while Oracle uses CVSS 3.1, so Oracle’s 8.1 maximum neither confirms nor rules out that CVE-2026-114938 is among the fixes. Oracle’s release notes for these builds do not name CVE-2026-114938. Oracle has not confirmed that CVE-2026-114938 is among the fixes, and other OpenJDK vendors (Temurin, Corretto, Zulu and others) release on their own schedules. [VERIFY @23:00 – confirm fixed versions per vendor]

How to mitigate Java4Shell before a patch is confirmed

No vendor-validated workaround has been published. It can be suggested to limit AVX usage or disable Base64 intrinsics as temporary measures. In HotSpot, the JVM option -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables the Base64 intrinsic entirely, while -XX:UseAVX=2 prevents the JVM from using the AVX-512 decoding path (on Java 21 and later the intrinsic remains active through its AVX2 path). These options exist in affected JDKs, but they have not been validated by Oracle or OpenJDK as a fix for this CVE, they may affect performance, and they do not replace patching. Recommended steps:

Inventory every Java runtime: OS packages, tarball/zip installs, JDKs bundled in applications and container base images, on both Linux and Windows.

Prioritize internet-facing Java services that decode untrusted Base64 input.

Apply vendor updates as soon as fixed builds for CVE-2026-114938 are confirmed, and rebuild container images on patched base images.

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, there are no reports of in-the-wild exploitation and no public proof-of-concept. Technical details are expected to become public within hours, which typically shortens the time to working exploits significantly. Organizations should treat this as urgent.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running potentially vulnerable Java versions across installation methods – OS packages, standalone JDK installations and JDKs bundled in container images – on both Linux and Windows. Customers can understand each asset’s exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk.

articles.title: How to Find Shadow AI Apps Built With AI App Builders
articles.context: The Orca Research Pod built and attacked real applications on several of these platforms, then measured which signals actually survive across templates and across our own...
articles.full_text:
Key findings: How to detect AI-built apps

Somebody in your organization has built an application with an AI app builder. It is running on one of your domains, it talks to a database holding real data, and it went through no procurement, no architecture review and no deployment process. You have no record of it because there was never a step at which a record would have been created.

From the outside these applications are close to invisible. They look like ordinary websites. Most of them run on the builder’s own infrastructure rather than in your estate, so there is no workload of yours to scan, and the ones that do reach a domain you own can be fronted through your own CDN, which erases the hosting fingerprint you would have matched on.

From the inside they are findable. The Orca Research Pod built and attacked real applications on several of these platforms, then measured which signals actually survive across templates and across our own customer fleet. Before you can secure these apps, you need to get visibility into AI systems running in your cloud, and these signals are where that starts. What works:

Packages the builder’s own scaffolding writes into the repositories it generates, some of which are provably inert anywhere else

Commit metadata, which is the most durable anchor available, because content gets edited and commit history does not

Build output that survives compilation into the files a visitor actually receives

DNS records on custom domains, though only some of them find anything

Cloud identities and resources a builder creates when a developer wires it to your own data services

Just as important is what does not work, because a detection rule built on the wrong signal produces noise that buries the real finding. We measured that too.

And the thing you are looking for is not the application on its own. It is the application together with the database behind it.

Signal 1: builder packages already in your software inventory

Start with packages, because you are almost certainly collecting them already.

One of the builders writes its own npm packages into the projects it generates. On its own that would not mean much, since a dependency list is full of things a developer chose deliberately. What makes these different is that they cannot function anywhere else. One of them activates only when a platform-specific environment variable is present, and renders only on that platform’s own domain.

Nobody would install it on purpose. It is residue. So if it is sitting in a repository in your estate, that project was created and run inside the builder.

That makes this the cheapest signal available. You are not adding a data source, you are writing a query against something you already have. Three details decide whether that query works.

Match any one of the packages, never all of them. The builder does not write an identical list into every project. Across three real applications, two of its packages appeared in all three, one appeared in a single project, and one in none. A rule that insists on the full set matches nothing at all.

Match the prefix, not the exact name. Package inventories commonly store the version inside the name, so an equality check silently returns zero and a perfectly good approach looks like a dead end.

Accept that one builder gives you nothing here. It ships no proprietary package whatsoever, and that is not a gap waiting to be filled, it is simply how the platform works. Its repositories carry one small configuration file and an HTML file with a default image URL. That is the entire surface.

Why builder names, editor libraries and HTTP headers produce false positives

Search for the builder’s name and you will find noise, occasionally spectacular noise.

One builder’s name is a common English word. A package with exactly that name appears in hundreds of organizations, and essentially every one of them is something else: a Linux device manager, an embedded key-value store, a chat framework, a ride-sharing company, a repository of torque specifications. Another builder’s name turned up in one company’s DNS as a run of records pointing at private addresses. Their internal naming scheme generates codenames as adjective plus adjective plus noun, and the builder’s name happened to sit on the adjective list.

The same vendor that writes those useful packages also publishes ordinary editor libraries that any developer might install. Those appear across many times more organizations than the proprietary ones do, and they indicate nothing whatsoever. A rule that counts them is measuring library popularity, not AI-generated software.

Then there is the shortcut that looks free: grep your stored HTTP response headers for builder names. Nothing new to collect, and the data is already there. When we measured it across the fleet, every single match was a Content Security Policy frame-ancestors entry, which means the site’s owner permits their own site to be embedded inside the builder’s interface. That is close to the opposite of what you wanted to know. It produces a list of companies that integrated with a builder, not companies that built something with one.

We dropped two header-based approaches for the same reason. Both told us where an application was hosted rather than who wrote it, and hosting turned out to imply the builder in a tiny fraction of cases.

Whole words and exact values, then. Never substrings. That one discipline is the difference between a rule your detection team keeps and a rule they mute within a week.

Signal 2: commit metadata and bot authors

Anything you can find inside a file has a shelf life. We know because our own research notes have been wrong twice in the same direction: markers we had treated as the primary tell for one builder are absent from every template we have generated since.

Commit metadata does not drift like that.

Two of the builders we studied commit generated code under a dedicated bot identity, one of them with more than 180,000 public commits to its name. A developer can open a generated file and delete a marker in ten seconds. Rewriting the authorship of an entire repository is a different kind of act, and almost nobody bothers.

Two things make this better than it first looks. In the AI-built repositories we examined, effectively every commit belonged to the bot, so the proportion of bot commits is a triage signal in its own right. When it sits at one, nobody has ever opened that application by hand.

And the baseline is clean. Across the distinct commit authors visible in our fleet data, not one was a bot of any kind. This is not a needle you have to separate from a haystack. There is no haystack.

Not every builder hands you this. One of them commits under the developer’s own identity and leaves nothing behind at all, which is worth knowing before you invest in collecting it.

Signal 3: builder markers that survive into compiled build output

A marker in a source tree tells you about a repository. A running application has been through a bundler, and most of what identified it in source is gone.

A few things do survive, and those are the ones that matter for anything already serving traffic. Across the builders we looked at, the survivors included a runtime error-reporting hook attached to the global object, asset URLs pointing back at the builder’s own domain, a default social-preview image URL, and, on one platform, a generator tag naming the builder in the page’s own metadata.

That last one is the best of them. It is a single line in an ordinary source file, it was present in both applications we generated on that platform, in source and in compiled output alike, and tens of thousands of public files carry it. It is also the one marker with no file of its own, which is why anyone auditing a repository by eye walks straight past it.

Which markers survive is specific to the template, and this is where re-verification matters most. Before you ship a rule, generate a fresh application on the platform and confirm your marker is still in the output. One of ours was not, and we only caught it because somebody rebuilt the test application instead of trusting notes written months earlier.

When you go looking, check application roots, web document roots, build output directories and container image layers. Then check user home directories, which is not optional. The real applications we studied lived under somebody’s home directory rather than in a tidy system path. Agentless scanning can read these locations, home directories included, without installing anything on the workload.

Signal 4: DNS records on custom domains

A custom domain gives you a DNS record to match, and for one builder that works well: your own records resolving into the platform’s dedicated address space, plus a verification record with a fixed prefix.

The detail worth carrying forward is which half of that does the work. Matching the builder’s hostname in DNS values found us a couple of organizations. Matching its dedicated addresses found an order of magnitude more.

For a builder with no address space of its own there is no equivalent. Its custom domains resolve into general-purpose cloud ranges shared with millions of other tenants, which you cannot match on without drowning in false positives, and its default hostnames live in the builder’s own zone, so they never enter your DNS at all. Until somebody pays for a custom domain, there is nothing there to see.

Signal 5: cloud identities that show an AI-built app’s blast radius

When a developer connects one of these builders to a data service in your own cloud, the builder provisions named artifacts inside your account. We reproduced this end to end across several integration paths: an identity holding read access to specific buckets, a query-service identity with permissions over a data catalog and a results bucket, catalog databases and tables describing your data, and, on another cloud, a service account with storage roles including one that could write.

What makes this the clearest evidence available is not that it names the builder. It is that the policy and the catalog entry tell you exactly which of your data an AI-generated application can reach. Every other signal in this post finds an application. This one measures the blast radius. Left unreviewed, a builder-created role can quietly join your list of overly permissive cloud identities.

It is also the least universal. One of the builders we studied provisions nothing in your cloud on any path, so there is no equivalent to go looking for.

Pair every AI-built app with the database behind it

What you are hunting is not the app on its own. It is the app together with the database behind it, and neither half is the risk by itself. Because the data is where the exposure lives, it pays to find and protect sensitive data across your cloud, so you already know what an AI-built app could reach when you find one.

Be careful how you find that second half, because a database client in a dependency list is not a database. Applications generated by one builder declare a client for a specific managed Postgres and then never use it, because it is template boilerplate rather than a decision. Of three real ones we took apart, one kept everything in memory, one used a completely different database, and one ran its own.

The reverse is just as common. An application on another platform that genuinely did have that managed Postgres attached carried no trace of the vendor anywhere in its source, because the connection string is injected at deploy time and the code only ever names an environment variable.

So the applications that declare a database and the applications that have one are two different sets, and neither bounds the other. Only an observed connection string or hostname proves the database is real. Whatever your rules record, give both halves a shared key from the start, so an analyst is handed one finding rather than two unrelated ones. Ours carries one, and it is the single field we refused to ship without.

It is worth being plain about severity, because it decides whether any of this is an alert or an inventory entry. A default-configured application on these platforms keeps its data off your premises with row-level security enabled, and does not leak on its own. Treat what you find as inventory and AI security posture management, not as an incident. Escalate when a builder artifact sits next to a secret on a scanned asset, or when the builder has been wired into your own cloud data. A database reachable through a generated function holding an administrative key, which is what we walked through in part 4 of this series, is a real finding. A generated to-do list is not. Drawing that line is how you prioritize the risks that matter most, instead of treating every generated app as an emergency.

A six-step checklist for finding AI-built apps in your estate

The platform-specific values are the one thing you have to supply, and all of them are either published or observable from a single generated application: the vendor’s package scope, its address ranges, its bot commit address, its asset domains.

Query your package inventory first. Prefix match, fire on any one of the set, and exclude the vendor’s general-purpose libraries.

Look for bot commit authors across your repositories, and treat a repository with a bot-only history as generated until somebody shows you otherwise.

Search your document roots and build outputs for the markers that survive compilation, not the ones that only ever existed in source.

Check DNS values against the builder’s address space, not just its hostname.

Audit your cloud for identities named after a builder that hold data permissions, then read the policy to see what they can reach. Whole words only.

Join every hit to its database, then re-verify your markers against a freshly generated application before you trust any of it. Ours drifted twice.

None of this is exotic work. The signals sit in data most estates already collect, and the reason these applications stay invisible is not that they hide well. It is that nobody has gone looking with the right query. The one thing that will not keep is the query itself, so whatever you build, put a date on it.

How Orca helps you find and secure AI-built apps

Everything above is a method you can run yourself, with queries you write and re-verify as the builders change. Orca AI AppGen Security helps you uncover apps built with AI tools and brings that discovery into the Orca Cloud Security Platform, so security professionals can protect builders and enable their organizations to grow using AI.

For every app it finds, Orca maps risk across the app’s APIs, integrations and data access. That keeps the application and the data behind it together as one finding, which is the pairing this research argues for.

Findings are prioritized by business impact in the same risk model as the rest of your cloud estate. A generated to-do list stays an inventory entry. A builder wired into production data moves to the top of the queue.

articles.title: CVE-2026-119618: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Race Condition Enables Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: The vulnerability was independently discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner (reported October 26, 2026) and Google Cloud Vulnerability Research (reported November 3, 2026),...
articles.full_text:
A critical vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server’s mod_http2 module, tracked as CVE-2026-119618 (CVSS 9.8), allows attackers to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on any server with HTTP/2 enabled. Because exploitation can lead to full server compromise without any authentication, immediate patching is required. The fix is Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71.

CVE-2026-119618 at a glance

CVE ID

CVE-2026-119618

Severity

CVSS 9.8 (Critical)

Weakness

Race condition (CWE-362) leading to heap memory corruption

Vulnerable component

assign_headers() function in mod_http2

Authentication required

None

Affected versions

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70; standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42

Fixed version

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71

Exploitation status

Reliable public exploit demonstrated; no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation at the time of writing

Temporary workaround

Disable HTTP/2 by removing h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive

What is CVE-2026-119618?

CVE-2026-119618 is a race condition in the assign_headers() function of mod_http2, the module that handles HTTP/2 in Apache HTTP Server. The function runs concurrently using shared resources without proper synchronization (CWE-362), and that gap leads to heap memory corruption.

How attackers exploit the mod_http2 race condition

Attackers send specially crafted HTTP/2 requests that trigger the race condition. The resulting heap corruption lets them execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the web server process, potentially leading to full infrastructure compromise. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

Which Apache HTTP Server versions are affected?

The following components are affected:

Apache HTTP Server mod_http2, versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70

Standalone mod_h2 releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42

Apache HTTP Server is one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world, and HTTP/2 can be enabled server-wide or per virtual host via the Protocols directive. That means a server can be exposed even if HTTP/2 was only switched on for a single site.

The standalone mod_h2 repository on GitHub has been archived since June 2026, so no standalone fix is available for those releases.

Is CVE-2026-119618 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default mod_http2 configuration, but no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

The vulnerability was independently discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner (reported October 26, 2026) and Google Cloud Vulnerability Research (reported November 3, 2026), underscoring the broad interest in this attack surface.

What can attackers do after exploiting CVE-2026-119618?

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to:

Execute arbitrary code on the web server

Pivot to internal networks and backend systems

Move laterally across the environment, potentially reaching full infrastructure compromise

The business consequences include service disruption and data exposure. Given the wormable potential of this flaw, due to the ubiquity of Apache HTTP Server and its unauthenticated attack surface, organizations should treat remediation as an urgent priority.

How to fix CVE-2026-119618

Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71

Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 immediately, prioritizing public-facing servers with HTTP/2 enabled. For standalone mod_h2 users, migrating to the bundled mod_http2 in Apache 2.4.71 is the recommended path forward.

Patch status by Linux distribution

Distribution

Status

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9

Fixed: mod_http2 update (RHSA-2026:98981)

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10

Fixed: mod_http2 update (RHSA-2026:98978)

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6, 7, and 8

Not affected

Debian unstable (sid)

Fixed: apache2 2.4.71-1

Debian bookworm, trixie, and forky

Vulnerable, no fix yet

Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview

Fix pending

Standalone mod_h2

No fix (repository archived); migrate to bundled mod_http2 in Apache 2.4.71

Temporary workaround: disable HTTP/2

If you can’t patch yet, administrators can disable HTTP/2 by removing h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving only http/1.1:

Protocols http/1.1

Note this may affect performance for HTTP/2-dependent clients. Check every virtual host as well as the server-wide configuration, since HTTP/2 can be enabled at either level. While patches roll out, keep watching exposed servers for unusual process activity and outbound connections, and use tools that detect and respond to cloud threats to catch post-exploitation behavior such as lateral movement.

How Orca helps you find and prioritize CVE-2026-119618 exposure

Using agentless scanning, Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Apache HTTP Server. From there, teams can understand their exposure in context (including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality) and prioritize the vulnerabilities that pose real risk rather than relying on CVSS alone.

Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first. With attack path analysis, teams can also see whether a vulnerable, internet-facing Apache server sits on a path to sensitive data or critical backend systems, which is exactly the pivot this vulnerability enables.

To see how Orca surfaces vulnerable Apache servers alongside the rest of your cloud risk in a unified cloud security platform, schedule a demo.

CVE-2026-119618 FAQ

Does CVE-2026-119618 affect Apache servers without HTTP/2 enabled?

The vulnerability sits in mod_http2, so exploitation requires HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server or on at least one virtual host. That is why removing h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive works as a temporary mitigation.

Which Apache version fixes CVE-2026-119618?

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes the vulnerability. Affected versions run from 2.4.55 through 2.4.70.

I run standalone mod_h2. Is there a patch?

No. The standalone mod_h2 repository has been archived since June 2026, so releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 won’t receive a standalone fix. Migrate to the mod_http2 module bundled with Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71.

Has CVE-2026-119618 been exploited in the wild?

Not as of this writing. A reliable public exploit has been demonstrated against a default mod_http2 configuration, so treat the risk as high, especially for internet-facing servers.

Which servers should I patch first?

Start with public-facing Apache servers that have HTTP/2 enabled, then servers that can reach sensitive data or backend systems. Exposure context matters more than the CVSS score alone when you’re deciding the order.

articles.title: See Your Cloud and Coding AI Agents in Context
articles.context: When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it
articles.full_text:
Securing AI in the cloud has historically meant securing models. Teams called Amazon Bedrock or Azure OpenAI, maybe hosted an open model on a GPU instance, and security’s job was to find those services, check their configurations, and keep training data from leaking.

AI Agents changed that. An agent takes the model’s output and acts on it. It calls tools, reads and writes data, opens tickets, runs code, and talks to other agents. To do any of that, it needs credentials and permissions. And in most organizations, nobody reviewed what those permissions are.

Orca now discovers the agents running in your cloud, both cloud-managed and self-hosted, including the coding agents your developers run on cloud infrastructure. The platform maps what each agent is connected to, and flags the agents that are misconfigured, over-privileged, or within reach of sensitive data.

Why are agents a different kind of AI risk?

A model’s risk is mostly about what it knows and what it says. An agent’s risk is about what it can do. That depends on four things that usually live in four different places:

The models it calls, managed or self-hosted.

The MCP servers it connects to, each exposing its own set of tools and running with its own credentials.

The identity it runs as, typically the IAM role or service account of the workload it lives on.

The data that identity can reach, from RAG sources and training buckets to production databases.

Agents also tend to blur identity lines. Many run under the same identity as the humans who use them, or inherit whatever role the host machine carries. When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it.

You can’t assess an agent just by looking at the agent. You have to see everything it’s connected to.

Why do existing tools miss it?

Most AI security tools see one layer. One inventories models. Another watches prompts. A third scans code. None of them knows that the LangChain agent on an EC2 instance is authenticated to an MCP server holding a Jira API token, or that its instance role can read an S3 bucket full of customer records.

Consider two agents running in the same account:

Agent A connects to a read-only documentation MCP server. Its workload role can reach one internal bucket of public product docs.

Agent B is a coding agent on a CI runner, configured to bypass permission checks so it runs commands with no human approval. It connects to an MCP server whose environment carries a CI/CD API token, and that server exposes tools like delete_bucket_object and revoke_db_access. The runner’s instance role can read a database containing PII.

An inventory lists both as “AI agent.” Only context tells you that one is a low-risk helper and the other is a path to your crown jewels.

Three Ways Orca Delivers AI Agent Security Posture

#1: Inventory as part of the AIBOM

Orca builds one inventory of every AI agent in your cloud, whether your teams use a managed agent platform or build their own.

Every agent appears in a new Agents tab in the AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM), filterable by account, cloud and framework, with new Agents widgets on the AI Security dashboard. Because SideScanning reads workload data out-of-band, there is nothing to install. No agents are required to find your agents.

AIBOM in the Orca Platform covering models, packages, MCP servers, and AI Agents

#2: Clear relationships in the Unified Data Model

Orca models every agent as a first-class asset in its Unified Data Model and links it to the things that define its risk:

The AI models it uses.

The MCP servers it connects to, whether local or remote, and the tools each server exposes.

The AI packages it was built with.

The IAM role it runs as, and the data stores that role can access.

Because these relationships sit in the same graph as the rest of your cloud, an agent’s blast radius is a question you can answer directly: what can this agent touch, and what could an attacker do with it?

An agent inventory tells you what exists. Agent context tells you what’s at stake.

See an AI agent’s connections to models, IAM roles, data stores, and policies in the Orca Platform.

#3: Prioritized risk in context

Orca adds new alerts built for agent risk: misconfiguration, over-privilege, reachable sensitive data, and runtime detections. Findings include:

AI agents authenticated to MCP servers that hold credentials, such as Jira, Confluence or Jenkins API tokens. A prompt injection against that agent inherits whatever the credential can reach.

AI agents configured to bypass permission checks, which removes the human approval step before the agent reads files, runs commands or calls tools.

MCP configuration files containing live secrets. Orca matches the secret value itself, so a hardcoded token is flagged and a safe environment-variable reference is not.

MCP servers communicating over plaintext HTTP to remote endpoints, exposing tool calls and their data in transit.

MCP tool sets that grant destructive tools such as deleting data, revoking access or terminating clusters.

Each alert includes plain-language remediation steps and is scored with Orca’s dynamic risk scoring, which weighs reachability, exploitability and blast radius rather than a static severity label. Agents can also serve as points in Orca’s attack path analysis, so an over-privileged agent two hops from a production database ranks above a misconfigured agent with nothing nearby.

Use Orca to see what an AI agent can access.

What about the coding agents your developers use?

Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI don’t only run on laptops. Teams run them on CI runners, cloud dev environments and build servers, where they pick up the host’s cloud credentials. Orca detects coding agents on cloud workloads the same way it detects any self-hosted agent, including the MCP servers they connect to and settings that turn off their approval prompts.

Coding agents also leave a second footprint: the code they write. Orca attributes code to the AI coding agents and models that wrote it, so you can see what share of your codebase is AI-generated, which repositories carry the most risk in AI-written code, and which models are linked to the most alerts.

Track the risk contributions of Coding Agents to improve their quality.

Visibility is half the job. Through Orca’s AI Skills Hub, you can plug skills and hooks into coding agents so they pull your security requirements, run AppSec scans, and fix issues to policy before code is committed.

One unified platform for cloud and AI risk

Agent findings land in the same alert workflows, integrations and dashboards your team already uses for the rest of your cloud. There is no separate AI console and no separate severity scale. The question every security team now has, “what are our agents doing and what can they reach?”, gets answered with the same context Orca already applies to workloads, identities and data.

Orca shows you every AI agent in your cloud, what it’s connected to, and which ones put sensitive data at risk, so your team can fix the riskiest agents first without slowing down the teams building them.

Want to see which agents are running in your cloud and how far they can reach? Book a personalized demo.

articles.title: Shadow AI Generated Apps: Find Them in the Cloud and Code You Already Scan
articles.context: The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026)
articles.full_text:
The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026). In 2025, CVE-2025-48757 showed how a single missing database policy in AI-generated Supabase projects exposed data across more than 170 production apps.

None of these apps went through a pull request or a security review. People outside engineering built them, often over a weekend, from accounts the security team had never seen.

When we introduced AI AppGen Security, we made the case that AI app builders turned every employee into a builder, and that the platforms those apps run on need security built for how they work. We started with integrations for Claude Enterprise and Vercel.

The first question we heard from security teams: how do I connect a platform I don’t know we use? Nobody files a ticket for a budget-forecasting app built on Lovable, and the marketing team’s campaign portal never reached architecture review. You can’t connect what you’ve never heard of.

AI app builders leave fingerprints in the DNS, workloads, code, and cloud identities Orca already scans agentlessly. Orca now flags them, so you can find AI-built apps nobody told you about and see what data they can reach. Below, we walk through why your current tools miss these apps, how Orca finds them, and what to do once you know.

Why the usual discovery paths miss AI-generated apps

You’d expect at least one of your existing tools to catch these apps. Here’s why none of them do.

Secure web gateways and CASBs see the visit, not the app. They can tell you an employee opened Lovable or Replit. They can’t tell you what was deployed, what data it holds, or whether it requires a login.

SSPM sees sign-ups through your identity provider. It reads IdP logs and OAuth grants, which shows the SaaS your employees signed up for with a work email. An app built from a personal account never touches your IdP.

AppSec scans the repositories you point it at. If a builder’s bot created the repo in a workspace security has never seen, nobody points anything at it.

Cloud security sees the evidence but doesn’t connect it to the service. A CNAPP already inventories the DNS record, the IAM user, and the package on the VM. Until now, a subdomain resolving into a builder’s IP range was just an address, and an IAM user created by an app builder was just an IAM user. The data was there. Nothing tied it to the service behind it.

Every one of these tools waits for someone to connect a system, a user, or a repo first. The apps that matter most are the ones nobody connected to.

How does Orca find apps nobody reported?

Services that run outside your environment still leave traces inside it. Orca already scans your cloud accounts, workloads, repositories, and external attack surface, so the traces are already in its data.

A fingerprint is an observed trace that ties an asset you own to an external service. Orca stores each one in its unified data model, where you can query it like any other asset. Each one records the service, the type of evidence, the exact value that matched, and when Orca first saw it.

To find these fingerprints, there’s no new agent to deploy, no vendor API to authorize, and nothing for the builder to opt into. Here’s where the evidence comes from:

Your external attack surface. DNS records whose values point into a builder’s or host’s infrastructure, vendor domain-verification records, and response headers showing a site is set up to load inside a builder’s live editor.

Your workloads. SideScanning already inventories installed packages and reads files across VMs and container images. Some builder packages only work inside the builder’s own development environment, so if one shows up on a workload, the project started there. File markers matter as much as packages, because production builds often strip out dependency manifests. Without file markers, package inventory can come back empty on the very images running an AI-built app.

Your code repositories. When an AI builder writes code, it commits under its own bot identity. That identity survives every human edit that follows, so the commit author is the most reliable sign a builder was involved.

Your cloud identities. When an app builder or its host connects to your cloud, it leaves an identity behind: an IAM user or role it authenticates as, a trust policy that lets it in, and a permissions policy naming what it can read. It’s also the only source that tells you what company data the service can reach.

Orca matches what a record points to, not what it’s called. A subdomain named lovable-test that points to a private IP doesn’t get flagged, and an app hosted on Vercel isn’t counted as built with v0. A discovery screen that flags every string with a vendor name in it gets muted within a week.

What can security teams do with the results?

Finding the app is the first step. Next you need to know what it can touch, and get it covered.

Detect: see every AI app service in use, and the evidence behind each one. Findings appear in three places:

AI AppGen Fingerprints have a dedicated Service Fingerprints view grouped by service type and then by service.

On each asset’s page, every fingerprint on that asset is listed with the value that matched.

Dashboard widgets summarize what’s detected, what’s connected, and posture for connected services.

How to find AI-built apps in your cloud environment with Orca. People across a company ship apps with AI app builders such as Lovable, v0, Bolt and similar tools, often without security teams knowing. This demo shows how Orca finds these apps and what they can reach. AI app builders leave evidence in cloud environments, code and DNS. Orca detects these fingerprints from data it already scans, with no agent, vendor API or opt-in required. Fingerprints are grouped by service, and the demo shows fingerprints from Base44, Supabase, Lovable and other AI platforms. For services that Orca integrates with, connect the account to secure the AI platform the same way the cloud is secured: identify issues, prioritize risk and implement remediation. Drill into the asset where a fingerprint was detected to see which other AI app services are tied to it. Set up dashboard widgets to track the footprint of AI-built apps in the cloud environment and manage risk while enabling AI innovation across the business. The demo ends with an invitation to discover shadow AI platforms in the cloud and to contact the Orca team to get started.

Connect: turn a finding into coverage. Where Orca supports a platform you haven’t connected, the fingerprint comes with a Connect action. Detection shows you which connections are worth making. Connecting turns on posture checks inside the platform, like flagging Supabase projects with row-level security turned off.

Why the evidence matters more than the count. Picture two Lovable apps, both found by Orca on the same day:

A marketing landing page. It has a DNS record pointing at the builder and nothing else: no cloud identity and no access to company data.

An internal expense tracker. It has the same DNS record, plus an IAM user Lovable created in your AWS account, with a policy that can read a bucket of customer records.

A tool that counts apps tells you there are 2. What you need to know is that one of them can read customer data.

That’s why the cloud identity fingerprint matters most to a CISO. The policy attached to a builder’s identity has a Resource element that names the buckets, datasets, and query workgroups it can reach.

Finding the AI app builder is only half the answer. The other half is naming the crown jewels the AI-built app can read.

Fingerprints are findings, not alerts. They don’t open alerts or change an asset’s risk score. They give you an inventory to govern from: decide which AI app builders your company allows, then use the Service Fingerprints view to spot the ones you don’t.

One limit to know about: DNS fingerprints cover only the zones Orca can read. The dashboard shows whether your DNS provider is connected, so a zone Orca can’t see never looks clean.

Which services does Orca detect?

Orca fingerprints these services:

AI app builders: Lovable, Vercel, v0, Replit, Base44, Netlify, and Bolt

Data services: Supabase

Where Orca has integrations set up with these services, security teams can connect and secure those AI platforms.

Your builders will keep shipping apps nobody asked security about. Now you’ll know when they do, and what those apps can reach.

Want to see which AI app builders are already running in your environment? Request a demo and we’ll walk you through it.

As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. articles.title: A Kubernetes CVE just dropped. Here’s how to find and fix what matters.
articles.context: ” Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access
articles.full_text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

articles.title: *sshole: OpenSSH Authentication Bypass Gives Attackers Root on Alpine Linux
articles.context: A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine
articles.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine. An unauthenticated attacker can log in over SSH password authentication as an account that should not accept passwords at all, including root. On a default Alpine install that means root access from a single connection, so patch now.

How the *sshole vulnerability bypasses SSH authentication

The bug comes from how musl libc’s crypt() reports errors. Since 2012, musl has returned the string “*” when crypt() fails instead of NULL, and its SHA-256 and SHA-512 crypt refuse passwords longer than 256 bytes. Locked and key-only accounts also use “*” as their shadow password field. When sshd checks passwords itself, without PAM, a password between 257 and 1024 bytes makes crypt() fail and return “*”. That matches the stored field, and sshd lets the attacker in.

Which locked and key-only accounts are exposed

Accounts exposed this way include root on Alpine 3.16 and later, key-only service and deploy users, directory users from nslcd, winbind or sssd, and the “alpine” user in tiny-cloud images, which has passwordless doas and is effectively root.

Which Alpine Linux and musl-based systems are affected

A system is affected when all of these hold: sshd is built without PAM (or runs with UsePAM no) on musl libc, PasswordAuthentication is on (the default), at least one account has “*” as its password field, and at least one local account has a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash. On Alpine that means the openssh-server package on releases 3.16 through 3.24 and edge. Other musl-based systems such as OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto builds, and container images that run sshd, may also be exposed. glibc distributions, PAM-enabled sshd, Dropbear and non-Linux systems are not affected.

How to patch *sshole: fixed OpenSSH versions and mitigations

Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2, or on Alpine to openssh 10.6_p2-r0 (edge), 10.3_p1-r2 (3.24), 10.2_p1-r1 (3.23), 10.0_p1-r11 (3.22), 9.9_p2-r1 (3.21) or 9.7_p1-r6 (3.20). Restart sshd afterwards, because upgrading the package does not replace the daemon that is already running. If you cannot patch yet, setting PasswordAuthentication no closes the hole. Also search authentication logs for “Accepted password for” on accounts that have no password, and treat any host with such a line as compromised.

Is *sshole being exploited in the wild?

The researcher’s public write-up explains the technique in enough detail to reproduce it, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported so far. Internet-facing Alpine hosts with password login enabled are the most exposed. An attacker who gets in this way has root on the host and can use it to reach the rest of the environment.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable OpenSSH hosts

Orca helps customers find assets running vulnerable OpenSSH versions and see each one’s exposure in context: whether it is reachable from the internet, at runtime, and how critical it is. Teams can use that context to fix the riskiest hosts first. Affected assets appear directly in the newItem view, so security teams can start with the most critical ones.

articles.title: Who Holds the Keys to Your ChatGPT Workspace?
articles.context: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal...
articles.full_text:
Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

Why nobody owns this

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

What Orca checks in ChatGPT Enterprise

You connect ChatGPT Enterprise to Orca with one read-only Admin API key. There’s nothing to install and no change to how anyone uses ChatGPT. Orca pulls in every user, group, service account, and service-account credential in the workspace, and flags issues like these out of the box:

Orca detects

Why it matters

A user with the workspace Owner role

Owners control every setting, member and key in the workspace. Each one is a high-value account

A workspace with more than three owners

Owner access tends to spread and rarely gets revoked. The same rule applies to Azure subscriptions and Supabase

A service-account credential with no expiration date

A token that never expires stays valid long after the job or person that needed it is gone

A service-account credential not rotated in 90 days

OpenAI suggests token lifetimes of 7 to 90 days. Older tokens have had more time to leak

A user not provisioned through the identity provider

Users added by hand skip your joiner-mover-leaver process, so offboarding may never reach them

A group managed by hand instead of synced from the identity provider

Manual groups drift from the access you approved in the IdP

A group with no members

Empty groups are leftovers that can quietly grant access to the next person added

Screenshot caption: A ChatGPT service-account credential with no expiration date, shown in Orca with its workspace, creation date and remediation steps.

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

That matters because OpenAI shows up in a lot more places than the ChatGPT admin console. At most companies, it looks something like this:

ChatGPT owners get reviewed in a spreadsheet once a quarter, if at all.

A DLP tool reads chats, a secrets scanner finds OpenAI API keys in repos, and the CNAPP covers Azure OpenAI.

Each tool sees its own piece, so nobody can say how exposed the company is to OpenAI overall. In Orca, ChatGPT users, groups, and credentials sit in the same inventory as OpenAI API keys found in code and container images, workloads calling OpenAI models (seen by the Orca Sensor), and Azure OpenAI resources. They land in the same queue as your Claude Enterprise and Vercel findings, too.

Screenshot caption: The Orca AI Security dashboard showing ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise workspaces side by side with cloud AI services.

The goal isn’t to slow anyone down. Your builders keep using ChatGPT the way they already do, and security finally gets a clear look at who holds the keys, without reading a single prompt.
